analysis.one_liner: Requires lenders to prove who owns a mortgage and document the borrower's situation before foreclosing.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or a floor action in the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: During the foreclosure crisis, this bill would have stopped any foreclosure on an owner-occupied home unless the foreclosing party first filed a report prepared by an independent party showing who actually holds the mortgage note, whether the loan and its servicing complied with federal consumer-protection laws, whether a real default occurred, and what modification options were offered. It also required written notice to the homeowner at least five days before foreclosure began, listing the homeowner's rights, deadlines, amounts owed, and workout options. The bill died in committee without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners facing foreclosure on their primary residences, especially those caught up in the mortgage-securitization system where loans were bought and sold so many times that no one could easily prove who held the note. The bill would have forced the foreclosing party to show it actually had the right to foreclose, disclosed any federal bailout money the parties received, documented compliance with consumer-lending laws, and given the homeowner a clear written account of options like modification before losing the home.

how_it_helps.text: Bars any foreclosure, judicial or nonjudicial, on an owner-occupied one- to four-family home unless the foreclosing party first files a detailed report identifying the actual holder of the mortgage note, the original lender, and all subsequent assignees.

Requires that report to be prepared by an independent party with no interest in the mortgage or foreclosure, and to assess compliance with laws including the Truth in Lending Act, RESPA, the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, and the Fair Housing Act, plus any violations that would justify letting the borrower rescind or redeem the loan.

Requires disclosure of whether any parties to the mortgage received federal assistance under the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act (the 2008 bank bailout) and how much, and a statement of whether a bona fide default actually occurred.

Requires written notice to the borrower at least five days before foreclosure action, covering the borrower's legal rights and deadlines, an itemized statement of amounts in arrears and reinstatement costs, and descriptions of modification, mitigation, and redemption options with correct contact information.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders, loan servicers, and foreclosure firms would bear the cost of preparing independent compliance reports, tracing the chain of ownership on securitized loans, and building in at least a five-day notice period. Some of those costs would likely be passed on through fees, and legitimate foreclosures would take longer and cost more to complete.

drawbacks.text: The reporting burden is heavy: every foreclosure would require an independent report assessing compliance with more than eight federal statutes, which would add cost and delay to foreclosures even where the default was genuine and uncontested, and lenders would likely pass those costs to borrowers through fees.

In the era of mortgage securitization, tracing the full chain of note holders and assignees was legally murky, so the ownership-identification requirement would likely have generated substantial litigation over whether each report was adequate, slowing every case.

A pre-foreclosure report documenting the borrower's race, gender, census tract, and income (as under the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act) would put sensitive personal data into court filings and state offices in every foreclosure case.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real, documented problem of the 2008-2010 period: foreclosures filed by parties who could not prove they held the note, and 'robo-signing' affidavits later exposed in congressional hearings and litigation. Requiring proof of ownership and a compliance report before taking someone's home is a protection most homeowners would want, and the five-day notice with itemized costs and workout information would have helped some borrowers avoid foreclosure entirely. The costs are real but mostly slow down and document a process that ends in losing a home; the bill was broad and paperwork-heavy, and a narrower version tied to demonstrating note ownership might have been easier to move, but no version ever got a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the two-year Congress without a hearing, a markup, or any vote.

narrative.text: Representative Marcy Kaptur introduced the bill on February 23, 2009, during the height of the foreclosure crisis, with Representative John Conyers joining her.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day, which was its only action; no subcommittee or full committee action, no report, and no floor vote ever followed.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor in the House in two years.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and servicers came out ahead: they kept the existing foreclosure process in place during the crisis, without having to prove note ownership, document compliance with consumer-protection laws, or provide the detailed pre-foreclosure notice the bill required. Homeowners facing foreclosure got no new federal protections from this bill.

for.name: John Conyers
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as its one cosponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 23, 2009, and never reported it out; no hearing or markup was held in the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had two Democratic sponsors and no Republican support on record, and it never advanced past committee, so no floor vote ever showed where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill would have forced servicers to prove who holds the note, document legal compliance, and disclose bailout assistance before foreclosing on a home, adding cost and delay to a high-volume process. Their interest in a fast, low-documentation foreclosure path ran against the homeowners' interest in verification and notice.

industries.industry: Banks and mortgage lenders (including securitization trusts)
industries.note: Originators and holders would have to disclose the full chain of assignment on securitized loans and any Emergency Economic Stabilization Act bailout funds received, and loans found noncompliant with consumer laws could expose borrowers to extended rescission or redemption rights. This was the paper trail the securitization industry had little incentive to produce.
